definition: A mathematical model for data types in which a data type is defined by its behavior (semantics) from the point of view of a user of the data, specifically in terms of possible values, possible operations on data of this type, and the behavior of these operations. This contrasts with data structures, which are concrete representations of data from the point of view of an implementer rather than a user.

One with only a signature and no implementation body. It is often used to specify that a subclass must provide an implementation of the method. Abstract methods are used to specify interfaces in some computer languages.

In software engineering and computer science, the process of removing physical, spatial, or temporal details or attributes in the study of objects or systems in order to more closely attend to other details of interest; it is also very similar in nature to the process of generalization. The result of this process is an abstract concept-object created by keeping common features or attributes to various concrete objects or systems of study.

A blueprint for software agents and intelligent control systems depicting the arrangement of components. The architectures implemented by intelligent agents are referred to as cognitive architectures.

A class of computational models for simulating the actions and interactions of autonomous agents with a view to assessing their effects on the system as a whole. It combines elements of game theory, complex systems, emergence, computational sociology, multi-agent systems, and evolutionary programming.
In database management, a function in which the values of multiple rows are grouped together to form a single value of more significant meaning or measurement, such as a sum, count, or max.

An approach to software development under which requirements and solutions evolve through the collaborative effort of self-organizing and cross-functional teams and their customers or end users. It advocates adaptive planning, evolutionary development, early delivery, and continual improvement, and it encourages rapid and flexible response to change.
An unambiguous specification of how to solve a class of problems. Algorithms can perform calculation, data processing, and automated reasoning tasks. They are ubiquitous in computing technologies.

A method or mathematical process for problem-solving and for engineering algorithms. The design of algorithms is part of many solution theories of operation research, such as dynamic programming and divide-and-conquer.

A property of an algorithm which relates to the number of computational resources used by the algorithm. An algorithm must be analyzed to determine its resource usage, and the efficiency of an algorithm can be measured based on usage of different resources.

A set of subroutine definitions, communication protocols, and tools for building software. In general terms, it is a set of clearly defined methods of communication among various components. A good API makes it easier to develop a computer program by providing all the building blocks.

Computer software designed to perform a group of coordinated functions, tasks, or activities for the benefit of the user. Common examples include word processors, spreadsheets, accounting applications, web browsers, media players, and photo editors.

A data structure consisting of a collection of elements, each identified by at least one array index or key. An array is stored such that the position of each element can be computed from its index tuple by a mathematical formula.

Intelligence demonstrated by machines, in contrast to the natural intelligence displayed by humans and other animals. AI research is defined as the study of intelligent agents, devices capable of perceiving their environment and taking actions that maximize the chance of successfully achieving their goals.

In computer programming, a statement that a predicate is always true at that point in code execution. It can help a programmer read the code, help a compiler compile it, or help the program detect its own defects.
An associative array, map, symbol table, or dictionary is an abstract data type composed of a collection of key-value pairs, such that each possible key appears at most once in the collection.
The study of abstract machines and automata, as well as the computational problems that can be solved using them. It is a theory in theoretical computer science and discrete mathematics.

An area of computer science and mathematical logic dedicated to understanding different aspects of reasoning. The study of automated reasoning helps produce computer programs that allow computers to reason completely, or nearly completely, automatically.
The maximum rate of data transfer across a given path. Bandwidth may be characterized as network bandwidth, data bandwidth, or digital bandwidth.
A formalism and a methodology for having a technique to specify probabilistic models and solve problems when less than the necessary information is available.

The act of running a computer program, a set of programs, or other operations, in order to assess the relative performance of an object, normally by running a number of standard tests and trials against it.

Expressions of what the resource usage is at least, at most, and on average, respectively, for a given algorithm. Best case is the function which performs the minimum number of steps; worst case performs the maximum number of steps; average case performs an average number of steps.
A term used to refer to data sets that are too large or complex for traditional data-processing application software to adequately deal with.
A mathematical notation that describes the limiting behavior of a function when the argument tends towards a particular value or infinity.
In mathematics and digital electronics, a number expressed in the base-2 numeral system, which uses only two symbols: typically 0 and 1.
A search algorithm that finds the position of a target value within a sorted array.
A tree data structure in which each node has at most two children, referred to as the left child and the right child.

An interdisciplinary field that combines biology, computer science, information engineering, mathematics, and statistics to develop methods and software tools for analyzing and interpreting biological data.
A basic unit of information used in computing and digital communications; a portmanteau of binary digit. A binary digit can have one of two possible values.
In telecommunications and computing, the number of bits that are conveyed or processed per unit of time.
In computing, a basic access control mechanism that allows through all elements except those explicitly mentioned in a list of prohibited elements.
A data type that has one of two possible values, usually denoted true and false, intended to represent the two truth values of logic and Boolean algebra.
An expression used in a programming language that returns a Boolean value when evaluated, that is one of true or false.
In mathematics and mathematical logic, the branch of algebra in which the values of the variables are the truth values true and false.
A unit of digital information that most commonly consists of eight bits, representing a binary number. Historically it was the number of bits used to encode a single character of text.
The procedures implemented in starting up a computer or computer appliance until it can be used. It can be initiated by hardware such as a button press or by a software command.
Any executable code that is passed as an argument to other code that is expected to call back and execute the argument at a given time.

The electronic circuitry within a computer that carries out the instructions of a computer program by performing the basic arithmetic, logic, controlling, and input/output operations specified by the instructions.
A unit of information that roughly corresponds to a grapheme, grapheme-like unit, or symbol, such as in an alphabet or syllabary in the written form of a natural language.
In cryptography, an algorithm for performing encryption or decryption, a series of well-defined steps that can be followed as a procedure.
In object-oriented programming, an extensible program-code-template for creating objects, providing initial values for state and implementations of behavior.
A piece of computer hardware or software that accesses a service made available by a server, often over a network.
Shared pools of configurable computer system resources and higher-level services that can be rapidly provisioned with minimal management effort, often over the internet.
A technique for implementing lexically scoped name binding in a language with first-class functions. A closure is a record storing a function together with an environment.
A collection of non-volatile resources used by computer programs, often for software development, including configuration data, documentation, pre-written code and subroutines.
A computer program that transforms computer code written in one programming language into another programming language, typically a lower-level language, to create an executable program.
Also known as recursion theory, a branch of mathematical logic and computer science that originated in the 1930s with the study of computable functions and Turing degrees.
Any type of calculation that includes both arithmetical and non-arithmetical steps and follows a well-defined model, such as an algorithm.
A subfield of computational science which focuses on classifying computational problems according to their inherent difficulty, and relating these classes to each other.
A set of rules and methods that describe the functionality, organization, and implementation of computer systems.
A digital telecommunications network which allows nodes to share resources, exchanging data using connections between nodes over cable or wireless media.
A collection of instructions that can be executed by a computer to perform a specific task.

The process of designing and building an executable computer program for accomplishing a specific computing task, involving analysis, generating algorithms, and implementation in a chosen programming language.
The theory, experimentation, and engineering that form the basis for the design and use of computers, involving the study of algorithms that process, store, and communicate digital information.
The protection of computer systems from theft or damage to their hardware, software, or electronic data, as well as from disruption or misdirection of the services they provide.
An interdisciplinary scientific field that deals with how computers can be made to gain high-level understanding from digital images or videos.
The process of joining together things. In computer programming, string concatenation is the operation of joining character strings end-to-end.
The ability of different parts or units of a program, algorithm, or problem to be executed out-of-order or in partial order, without affecting the final outcome.
A feature of a programming language which performs different computations or actions depending on whether a programmer-specified Boolean condition evaluates to true or false.
A class, data structure, or abstract data type whose instances are collections of other objects, storing them in an organized way that follows specific access rules.
Producing software in short cycles with high speed and frequency so that reliable software can be released at any time, with a simple and repeatable deployment process.
The practice of integrating source code changes frequently and ensuring that an integrated codebase is in a workable state.
The order in which individual statements, instructions or function calls of an imperative program are executed or evaluated.
The practice and study of techniques for secure communication in the presence of third parties called adversaries, including data confidentiality, data integrity, authentication, and non-repudiation.
A process of discovering patterns in large data sets involving methods at the intersection of machine learning, statistics, and database systems.
An interdisciplinary field that uses scientific methods, processes, algorithms, and systems to extract knowledge and insights from data in various forms, structured and unstructured.
A data organization, management, and storage format that enables efficient access and modification, comprising a collection of data values, relationships, and applicable operations.
An attribute of data which tells the compiler or interpreter how the programmer intends to use the data, constraining the values an expression might take.
The process of finding and resolving defects or problems within a computer program that prevent correct operation of computer software or the system as a whole.
In computer programming, a language construct that specifies properties of an identifier, declaring what a word means, most commonly for functions, variables, constants, and classes.
A field of computer science that studies distributed systems, whose components are located on different networked computers that communicate and coordinate actions by passing messages.
An algorithm design paradigm based on multi-branched recursion, working by recursively breaking down a problem into two or more sub-problems until simple enough to be solved directly.
A hierarchical and decentralized naming system for computers, services, or other resources connected to the internet or a private network, translating domain names to numerical IP addresses.
The process of encoding information, converting plaintext into an alternative form known as ciphertext so that only authorized parties can decipher it back to the original information.
A programming paradigm in which the flow of the program is determined by events such as user actions, sensor outputs, or messages from other programs or threads.
The process of responding to the occurrence of exceptions, anomalous or exceptional conditions requiring special processing that often disrupt the normal flow of program execution.
Causes a computer to perform indicated tasks according to encoded instructions, as opposed to a data file that must be parsed by a program to be meaningful.
In a programming language, a combination of constants, variables, operators, and functions that the language interprets and computes to produce another value.
A control flow statement for specifying iteration, which allows code to be executed repeatedly.
The act of proving or disproving the correctness of intended algorithms underlying a system with respect to a certain formal specification, using formal methods of mathematics.
A programming paradigm that treats computation as the evaluation of mathematical functions and avoids changing-state and mutable data.
A term used to describe the concept that flawed or nonsense input data produces nonsense output, and can also refer to poorly written programs producing nonsensical behavior.
In computer programming, a variable with global scope, meaning that it is visible and accessible throughout the program unless shadowed.
The study of graphs, mathematical structures used to model pairwise relations between objects, made up of vertices connected by edges.
A function that can be used to map data of arbitrary size to data of a fixed size, often used with a hash table to accelerate data lookup.
A data structure that implements an associative array abstract data type, using a hash function to compute an index into an array of buckets from which a value can be found.
A specialized tree-based data structure which is essentially an almost complete tree satisfying the heap property regarding parent and child node values.
Research into the design and use of computer technology, focused on the interfaces between people and computers, situated at the intersection of computer science, behavioral sciences, and design.
In computer languages, tokens which name language entities such as variables, types, labels, subroutines, and packages.
A programming paradigm that uses statements that change a program's state, focused on describing how a program operates through commands.
In object-oriented programming, the mechanism of basing an object or class upon another object or class, retaining similar implementation and forming a hierarchy of classes.
The communication between an information processing system, such as a computer, and the outside world, involving signals or data received and sent.
A simple sorting algorithm that builds the final sorted array or list one item at a time.
A software application that provides comprehensive facilities to computer programmers for software development, normally consisting of a source code editor, build automation tools, and a debugger.
The phase in software testing in which individual software modules are combined and tested as a group, occurring after unit testing and before validation testing.
A high-level, interpreted programming language originally built for adding interactivity to web pages, now also widely used on servers through runtimes like Node.js.
A database operation that combines rows from two or more tables based on a related column between them, commonly used to pull related data together in a single query.
The core component of an operating system, managing communication between hardware and software, handling memory, processes, and device control at the lowest level.
A type of database that stores data as a simple collection of key and value pairs, optimized for fast lookups rather than complex relational queries.
The delay between a request being made and the corresponding response being received, often measured in milliseconds in networking and computing contexts.
A linear data structure where each element, called a node, points to the next node in the sequence, allowing efficient insertion and deletion without shifting elements.
The practice of distributing computing workloads across multiple servers or resources to optimize performance, maximize throughput, and avoid overloading any single resource.
A subfield of artificial intelligence in which systems learn patterns from data and improve their performance on a task without being explicitly programmed for every rule.
A software bug where a program fails to release memory it no longer needs, gradually consuming more resources over time and potentially degrading performance or crashing.
Data that describes other data, such as a file's creation date, author, or format, providing context without being part of the primary content itself.
Software that acts as a bridge between different applications or between an operating system and applications, handling communication and data management between them.
A technique where a program executes multiple threads concurrently within a single process, allowing tasks to run in parallel and make better use of processor resources.
A container that provides context for identifiers, allowing the same name to be used in different namespaces without conflict, commonly used to organize code.
A computing system loosely inspired by the human brain, made up of layers of interconnected nodes that learn to recognize patterns by adjusting connection weights during training.
The process of organizing a relational database's tables and columns to reduce data redundancy and improve data integrity, typically by splitting data into related tables.
A programming paradigm based on the concept of objects, which bundle data and behavior together, supporting principles like encapsulation, inheritance, and polymorphism.
Software whose source code is made publicly available for anyone to view, use, modify, and distribute, usually under a license that governs how it can be reused.
System software that manages computer hardware and software resources and provides common services for computer programs, sitting between applications and the hardware.
A modeling error in machine learning where a model learns the training data too closely, including its noise, resulting in poor performance on new, unseen data.
A formatted unit of data carried by a packet-switched network, containing both the payload being transmitted and control information such as source and destination addresses.
A type of computation in which many calculations or processes are carried out simultaneously, often by splitting a large problem into smaller ones solved at the same time.
The process of analyzing a sequence of symbols, such as source code or text, according to the rules of a formal grammar to determine its structure.
A decentralized network architecture in which participating computers, called peers, share resources directly with each other without relying on a central server.
In object-oriented programming, the ability of different classes to be treated as instances of the same general type through a shared interface, while behaving differently.
A defined set of rules that governs how data is formatted, transmitted, and received between devices on a network, ensuring different systems can communicate reliably.
A request for information from a database, typically written in a query language such as SQL, that specifies the data to retrieve, filter, or modify.
A linear data structure that follows the First-In-First-Out (FIFO) principle, where elements are added at one end and removed from the other.
A flaw in a system where the outcome depends on the uncontrollable timing of events, such as multiple threads accessing shared data simultaneously in an unintended order.
A programming technique in which a function calls itself to solve smaller instances of the same problem, continuing until a base case is reached.
The process of restructuring existing computer code without changing its external behavior, done to improve readability, reduce complexity, or make future changes easier.
A type of software testing performed to confirm that recent code changes have not adversely affected existing features that previously worked correctly.
A database that organizes data into tables of rows and columns, with relationships between tables defined through keys, typically queried using SQL.
An architectural style for designing networked applications, relying on stateless communication and standard HTTP methods to allow systems to interact over the web.
An application programming interface that follows REST principles, allowing clients to access and manipulate resources through standard HTTP requests like GET and POST.
The process of analyzing a system, device, or piece of software to understand how it works, often without access to its original design documentation or source code.
The period during which a program is actively executing, as well as the environment or system that supports a program's execution, managing memory and resources.
The capability of a system to handle a growing amount of work, or its potential to be enlarged to accommodate that growth, by adding resources.
A programming language designed for automating tasks that would otherwise be performed manually, typically interpreted rather than compiled, such as Python or Bash.
An extension of the World Wide Web that aims to make data understandable by machines, not just humans, through standards that describe relationships between data.
A computer program or device that provides functionality, data, or services to other programs or devices, called clients, typically over a network.
A structured process that outlines the stages involved in developing software, from initial planning and design through implementation, testing, deployment, and maintenance.
An algorithm that arranges elements of a list or array in a particular order, typically numerical or lexicographical, such as quicksort, mergesort, or bubble sort.
Structured Query Language, a standard programming language used to manage and manipulate relational databases, allowing users to query, insert, update, and delete data.
A linear data structure that follows the Last-In-First-Out (LIFO) principle, where the most recently added element is the first one removed.
A type-checking approach in which variable types are known and verified at compile time rather than at runtime, catching certain errors before the program runs.
A logical subdivision of an IP network, used to split a larger network into smaller, more manageable segments for organizational or performance reasons.
The foundational suite of communication protocols used to interconnect network devices on the internet, defining how data is packetized, addressed, and delivered.
The smallest sequence of programmed instructions that can be managed independently by a scheduler, typically existing as part of a larger process.
A measure of the amount of time an algorithm takes to run as a function of the size of its input, commonly expressed using Big O notation.
A sequence of database operations that are treated as a single logical unit of work, either completing entirely or not at all, to preserve data consistency.
An ordered, typically immutable collection of elements, which may be of different types, commonly used to group related values together.
A software testing method where individual components or functions of a program are tested in isolation to verify that each performs as expected.
Uniform Resource Locator, a reference that specifies the location of a resource on the internet along with the protocol used to access it, such as https.
The space where interactions between humans and a machine occur, encompassing the visual elements, layouts, and controls a user interacts with.
A system that records changes to files over time, allowing developers to track revisions, collaborate, and revert to previous versions when needed, such as Git.
A software-based emulation of a physical computer, capable of running an operating system and applications as if it were a separate physical machine.
The creation of a virtual version of a resource, such as a server, storage device, or network, allowing multiple virtual instances to run on shared physical hardware.
Virtual Private Network, a technology that creates a secure, encrypted connection over a public network, allowing users to send and receive data as if directly connected.
A linear, sequential approach to software development where each phase, such as requirements, design, implementation, and testing, must be completed before the next begins.
Software or hardware that serves content, typically web pages, to clients over the internet using protocols such as HTTP, responding to browser requests.
An access control mechanism that permits only explicitly approved items, such as email addresses or applications, while blocking everything else by default.
Extensible Markup Language, a markup language designed to store and transport structured data in a format that is both human-readable and machine-readable.
A human-readable data serialization format commonly used for configuration files, relying on indentation rather than brackets to represent structure.
A software security flaw that is unknown to the vendor or has no available fix at the time it is discovered or exploited, leaving systems exposed until patched.
